# Engine for Briggs & Stratton mower not starting. Might be flooded

If your Briggs & Stratton mower refuses to crank or fire up immediately after refueling, and you suspect a fuel flood, the symptoms are distinct from a simple lack of ignition. The specific detail providedâthat gas is leaking from the air filterâconfirms that the carburetor bowl has exceeded its capacity. In this scenario, liquid fuel has risen above the float level, pushing past the needle valve seal and migrating into the intake tract. This isn't just a case of "wet spark plug"; it is an overflow condition that introduces unmeasured fuel directly into the cylinder.

When you attempt to start the engine, the carburetor's internal float mechanism relies on buoyancy to regulate fuel flow. If the bowl is overfilled, the float cannot submerge enough to close the needle valve. Consequently, fuel continues to drip or stream into the carburetor throat even when the throttle is closed. This excess liquid bypasses the metering jets and enters the crankcase via the air filter assembly. The result is a cylinder flooded with a rich mixture of gasoline and air, displacing the oxygen required for combustion.

### Immediate Intervention: Cranking Strategy

The most effective mechanical intervention in this state is to remove the spark plug wire and attempt to crank the engine without ignition. This action acts as a manual purge valve. As the piston compresses the flooded mixture during the compression stroke, it forces the liquid out through the path of least resistanceâtypically the exhaust port or back into the carburetor throat if the intake is blocked by the air filter housing.

If you leave the spark plug connected, the engine may momentarily catch due to the sheer volume of fuel, only to stall violently once the mixture becomes too lean as the fuel drains away or if the cylinder wall becomes coated in oil diluted by excess gasoline. By disconnecting the high-tension wire, you ensure that the energy from the starter motor is entirely dedicated to physically expelling the fluid rather than attempting a failed combustion event. Listen for the distinct "pop" of air and vapor escaping from the exhaust; this indicates the cylinder is clearing.

### Carburetor Bowl Drain and Inspection

Once the initial cranking has occurred, you must address the source of the leak: the overfilled carburetor bowl. Locate the drain screw on the bottom of the carburetor body (usually a small hex head near the fuel line connection). Unscrew this until all liquid drains out into a safe container. Do not skip this step; residual fuel in the bowl will continue to seep through the needle valve if the float is compromised or if the fuel level was pushed too high by an overfill event.

Inspect the float and the needle valve while the bowl is open. The needle valve is a simple tapered stem that seats into a matching port on the carburetor body. If it feels sticky or does not seat flush, debris from the tank may be preventing a seal. Clean both components with solvent and dry them thoroughly. A common pitfall here is assuming the fuel pump is at fault when the issue is purely mechanical overflow. However, if the float itself is filled with gas or the needle valve is bent, normal refilling will result in a repeat of this leak.

### Air Filter Housing Dynamics

Regarding the gasoline leaking from the air filter: this confirms that the liquid has traveled up the intake manifold and pooled around the spark plug well. The air filter housing acts as a reservoir in this state. If you leave the mower sitting, the fuel can soak into the foam or paper elements of the filter, creating a secondary ignition hazard.

Before reinstalling the air filter, ensure the carburetor throat is dry to the touch. Reinstalling a wet filter on top of a flooded intake will only reintroduce liquid into the cylinder. If the liquid has soaked deeply into the foam, it may be prudent to replace the filter rather than attempting to dry it, as saturated foam loses its filtration efficiency and can allow oil or unburned fuel particles to enter the combustion chamber, leading to fouling of the spark plug even after the engine starts.

### Refueling Protocol

Once the system is drained and cleared, refuel with caution. A Briggs & Stratton carburetor bowl has a finite volume, typically around 15 to 20 milliliters depending on the specific model series. Overfilling the main tank forces fuel past the overflow tube or through the needle valve if the float height is incorrect. When filling the tank, stop well before the cap is reached. The reserve tank in many older models relies on gravity feed; overfilling here can also trigger unintended siphoning effects that exacerbate flooding issues during operation.

If the engine still fails to start after draining and refilling, check the spark plug gap with a feeler gauge. A flooded mixture can wash away the oil film from the cylinder walls, causing increased friction or scoring if the engine runs lean upon restart. Ensure the new spark plug is gapped correctly for the specific ignition timing requirements of the Briggs & Stratton unit to prevent misfiring under load.
